title: The everything theory of mass transit - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: American public transit is burdened with goals it was never designed for (emissions, union jobs, community input, electrification), and each extra mandate trades off against its core job of moving people. The author argues that congestion pricing, higher service frequency, and denser land use cut emissions far more efficiently than electrifying buses, while mission creep hurts the poor who depend on transit most.

insights.claim: Public transit is asked to solve problems it was never designed for (cutting emissions, beautifying neighborhoods, adding union jobs, reflecting community input), and every extraneous goal costs money and adds delay that impedes moving people.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Frames transit underperformance as a governance/incentive problem, not a funding shortfall, relevant to how infrastructure dollars actually convert to service.
insights.locator: We ask public transport to address problems

insights.claim: The Transit Costs Project documents that the Boston Green Line extension, finished a decade late, added a three-kilometer bike and pedestrian path costing $20 million after just 13 people advocated for it at a community meeting.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A concrete example of how community-input mandates inflate US transit capital costs, the core reason American projects cost multiples of peer nations'.

insights.claim: Buses face more rules and regulations than personal cars despite accounting for less than one percent of US transportation emissions, while road and highway building stays focused on its primary mobility mandate.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Highlights a regulatory asymmetry that structurally disadvantages transit versus cars, a fixed headwind for transit-agency economics.
insights.quote: Buses are a rounding error as a proportion of vehicles on the road, accounting for less than one percent of US transportation emissions.

insights.claim: Transit's goals only crept after governments took over languishing private lines in the 1960s, creating reliance on taxpayer subsidies from a mostly-driving public whose non-user interests then had to justify the funding.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Explains the political root of mission creep: subsidy from non-users forces transit to sell benefits beyond ridership, embedding the inefficiency.

insights.claim: Each level of government layers on more requirements (Buy America domestic sourcing, CHIPS-style daycare, Davis-Bacon prevailing wages, California Environmental Quality Act review, local art and hiring rules), compounding cost onto a single transit project.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Maps the stacked-mandate mechanism that makes US infrastructure slow and expensive, a durable friction for any transit or public-works exposure.
insights.locator: The typical transit agency gets funding

insights.claim: While 91.5 percent of American households own at least one car, less than half (45 percent) of transit riders have a vehicle available at home, so extraneous transit goals trade off against the welfare of the poor who use it most.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Quantifies transit's captive low-income ridership, the group most harmed when mandates divert money from frequency and coverage.
insights.quote: While 91.5 percent of American households own at least one car, less than half (45 percent) of transit riders have a vehicle available to them at home.

insights.claim: In most of the US, not having a car worsens poverty: poor people who gain car access are more likely to find and keep jobs, earn more, work more hours, get off welfare, and move to better neighborhoods.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Reframes cars, not just transit, as an anti-poverty tool, undercutting the assumption that transit spending is inherently pro-poor.
insights.locator: In most of the US, not having a car makes poverty worse

insights.claim: Battery electric buses cost far more to buy and maintain: Austin's CapMetro 40-foot electric buses cost $917,000 versus $535,000 for diesel, and Miami-Dade paid roughly $1.1 million per electric bus.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Hard cost deltas show electrification mandates directly shrink service budgets, a bearish signal for agency-funded EV bus demand economics.
insights.locator: Battery electric buses cost more to procure

insights.claim: Of Miami-Dade's 75 electric buses only about six run on a given day because they break down every 600 miles (seven times as often as diesel) and parts are scarce after manufacturer Proterra's bankruptcy.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Reliability collapse and a bankrupt supplier illustrate the operational and supply-chain risk in current US electric-bus procurement.
insights.locator: That’s because the electric buses break down

insights.claim: Buy American rules make US electric buses cost nearly twice Europe's, where Chinese manufacturers compete freely and a standard 12-meter electric bus sells for roughly $600,000; only about 7,000 of ~63,000 US buses are electric, 5,000 of them school buses.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Protectionism roughly doubles US electric-bus prices and keeps the market small and uncompetitive, a structural drag on domestic transit electrification.
insights.locator: The problem is even worse in the United States

insights.claim: The money to electrify one bus, at a US median $131 per operating hour and 14.3 passengers per hour, could instead fund roughly 2,300 additional service hours carrying at least 30,000 more riders.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Quantifies the opportunity cost of electrification versus service, the author's central efficiency argument for reallocating capital.
insights.quote: the money for electrifying one bus could fund roughly 2,300 additional service hours, carrying at least 30,000 additional riders
insights.locator: Assuming the median cost per hour

insights.claim: Research on Stockholm's busiest bus route found that better road and transit pricing plus more frequent buses yielded more benefit than electrifying buses, which raise operator costs by at least 16 percent while being identical from a passenger view.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Evidence that pricing and frequency, not electrification, are the efficient emissions levers, redirecting where climate transit dollars should go.

insights.claim: London's congestion charge cut vehicle greenhouse gas emissions by 16 percent, generated £227 million in a year, and reduced traffic accidents by nine percent in its first year.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A proven, revenue-positive policy that outperforms electrification on emissions, strengthening the case for pricing over vehicle subsidies.

insights.claim: Increasing transit service frequency by 1 percent boosts ridership by about 0.5 percent, and once buses arrive every ten minutes service becomes appealing to riders who have alternatives, creating a positive feedback loop of revenue and quality.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: The frequency-ridership elasticity is the mechanism by which mode-shift, not electrification, produces durable emissions cuts.
insights.quote: increasing transit service frequency by 1 percent boosts ridership by about 0.5 percent

insights.claim: Switching people from driving to transit saved nine million metric tons of carbon in 2018, but decreasing travel distances through more efficient land use could prevent 66 million metric tons.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Land-use density dwarfs mode-shift as an emissions lever, pointing climate value toward zoning and development rather than fleet purchases.
insights.locator: Switching people from driving to transit saved

themes.theme: Broad-base behavior change over burdening the poor

insights.claim: A 2018 UCLA report estimated that if one in four rare transit users replaced a single driving trip with transit every two weeks, annual ridership in Southern California would grow by 96 million.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Small behavior change across a broad base beats forcing burdened low-income riders to carry the emissions load, reframing where transit policy should aim.
insights.quote: if just one in every four people who rarely rides transit replaced a single driving trip with transit every two weeks, annual ridership would grow by 96 million
insights.locator: A 2018 UCLA report on transit ridership
